## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Geometry Processing and Geometric Deep Learning
  Official title       Geometry Processing and Geometric Deep Learning
  Instructors          E. CORMAN, J.DIGNE, M. OVSJANIKOV (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 26 h (lectures 12 h, labs 14 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Deep Learning, Geometry
  Language             Course materials in English; the course may be given in English if there is a non-French speaker in the class (master-mva.com)
  Assessment           Practical sessions (TPs); mini quizzes (15 minutes every 2 lectures); final projects (implement a paper from a list proposed by the instructors) (master-mva.com). Université Paris-Saclay course detail: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (partial continuous assessment). Weights: not displayed.
  Prerequisites        Not displayed
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with an M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who knows linear algebra, multivariable calculus and the basics of neural networks, and who wants to analyse, match, learn on and generate 3D shapes.

**Empirical first**: a body scanned in two poses has completely different $(x, y, z)$ coordinates but almost the same geodesic distances *on* the surface, so a network built from the Laplace–Beltrami operator is blind to the pose, while a coordinate-based one must learn every pose. The same operator makes a network indifferent to the mesh: trained on an 800-vertex mesh, the small network of Code 7.9 reaches 96 % accuracy on a 2500-vertex mesh of the same surface that it never saw.

The course builds the calculus of surfaces on triangle meshes (gradients, Laplacians, curvature, geodesics), uses it to deform, flatten and match shapes, turns the same operators into network layers, and ends with neural fields and generative models. It complements [Geometric Data Analysis](../s1-geometric-data-analysis/index.html) (distances between shapes), [Point Clouds and 3D Modelling](../s2-point-clouds-3d/index.html) (acquisition and reconstruction) and [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html) (learning on grids).

### What you will be able to do

-   Assemble the cotangent Laplacian, the mass matrix, the gradient and the divergence of a triangle mesh from the finite element method, and state their properties.
-   Compute heat diffusion, geodesic distances with the heat method, and spectral filters on a surface.
-   Compute discrete mean and Gaussian curvature and prove the discrete Gauss–Bonnet theorem.
-   Build the heat, wave and global point signatures and explain why they are invariant to isometries.
-   Deform a mesh with the as-rigid-as-possible energy and flatten a disk-like mesh with Tutte's method, and explain the topological obstructions to flattening.
-   Compute a functional map between two shapes and convert it into a point-to-point correspondence.
-   Define parallel transport on a mesh, prove that its holonomy equals the angle defect, and build gauge-equivariant layers.
-   Compare PointNet, graph networks, MeshCNN, SpiralNet++, DiffusionNet and DeltaConv, and train an operator-based network.
-   Fit neural signed distance fields with Fourier features, SIREN and eikonal regularisation, and write the NeRF rendering equation.
-   Explain how meshes are generated and made differentiable, and fit a template mesh to a point cloud.
-   Reimplement a research paper of the field and evaluate it, as the course project asks.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com sets the objective of introducing advanced topics in modern geometric data analysis, the field known as Geometry Processing. It focuses on mathematical foundations (discrete differential geometry, mapping, optimization) and on the deep learning methods that perform best.

The description announces an overview of surface-based analysis and processing, then modern deep learning techniques for 3D shape classification, correspondence and parametrization, and finally recent approaches for generating geometry from both the mesh and the shape perspectives. ### Course outline

-   **Review: calculus on surfaces, linear algebra and convolution** — the metric, the Laplace–Beltrami operator, Green's formula, generalised eigenproblems, a 1D finite element model, convolution and equivariance.
-   **Triangle meshes and discrete differential operators** — meshes, hat functions, mass and stiffness matrices, the cotangent Laplacian, gradient and divergence.
-   **Heat diffusion, geodesics and convolution on surfaces** — the heat equation, Varadhan's formula, the heat method, and filters that act as convolutions.
-   **Spectral geometry, curvature and spectral signatures** — manifold harmonics, mean and Gaussian curvature, Gauss–Bonnet, HKS, WKS and GPS.
-   **Deformation, parameterization and topology** — Laplacian editing, as-rigid-as-possible deformation, Tutte and conformal maps, topological obstructions and toric covers.
-   **Maps between surfaces and shape matching** — pointwise and functional maps, their computation from descriptors, spectral upsampling.
-   **Deep learning on curved surfaces** — spectral and geodesic CNNs, parallel transport, holonomy, gauge-equivariant and rotation-equivariant features.
-   **Architectures and applications** — coordinate systems, PointNet, graph networks, MeshCNN, SpiralNet++, DiffusionNet, DeltaConv; classification, segmentation, correspondence.
-   **Neural fields for surfaces** — SDFs and occupancy, DeepSDF, occupancy networks, Fourier features, SIREN, eikonal regularisation, NeRF, implicit displacement fields.
-   **Generative modelling of geometry** — Chamfer losses, texture synthesis and in-painting, mesh generation, differentiable meshing, Point2Mesh.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — learned correspondence, equivariance, new neural representations and 3D generation (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read [ch. 0](#ch0) first even if the material looks familiar: Green's formula and the generalised eigenproblem return in every later chapter.
-   Keep one mental picture: almost everything in the course is built from two sparse matrices, the stiffness $L$ and the mass $M$ of [ch. 1](#ch1).
-   After each session, run the code of the chapter and change one parameter (the diffusion time, the number of eigenfunctions, the regularisation weight) to see what breaks.
-   Do the exercises listed in the session plan before the next session; the ★★★ ones are good starting points for the project.
-   Python environment: NumPy, SciPy (`scipy.sparse`, `scipy.sparse.linalg.eigsh`, `scipy.spatial`) and PyTorch on CPU. Every code block builds its own synthetic mesh and runs in under 30 seconds on a laptop; “Code N.k” means the code of Example N.k.
-   For real data, read meshes with a library such as `trimesh` or `libigl`, and inspect them in a mesh viewer such as MeshLab. Public benchmarks include FAUST (Bogo et al., 2014) and ModelNet40 (Wu et al., 2015).
-   Start choosing a paper for the project around session 5: the [solo subjects](#projects-solo) show the scale to aim at.

## 0. Review: calculus on surfaces, linear algebra and convolution {#ch0}

Every later chapter differentiates functions on a surface, integrates them, and solves eigenvalue problems with two matrices. This review recalls the smooth objects that the discrete operators imitate, and the linear algebra that computes them.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Regular surface, metric and area]{.tag} A **regular patch** is a smooth map $x : U \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ whose Jacobian $J = (\partial_1 x, \partial_2 x)$ has rank 2. The tangent plane $T_p S$ is spanned by $\partial_1 x$ and $\partial_2 x$, and the unit normal is
$$
n = \frac{\partial_1 x \times \partial_2 x}{\|\partial_1 x \times \partial_2 x\|}.
$$

The **metric** (first fundamental form) is the $2 \times 2$ matrix $g = J^\top J$, with entries $g_{ij} = \langle \partial_i x, \partial_j x \rangle$. It gives lengths of curves and the area element:
$$
\mathrm{d}A = \sqrt{\det g}\; \mathrm{d}u^1 \mathrm{d}u^2 .
$$

A quantity is **intrinsic** when it depends on $g$ only. It is then unchanged by any isometry, a deformation that preserves the lengths of all curves on the surface, such as bending a sheet of paper.
:::

::: def
[Definition 0.2 — Gradient, divergence, Laplace–Beltrami]{.tag} For $f : S \to \mathbb{R}$, the **gradient** $\nabla f$ is the tangent vector such that $\langle \nabla f, v \rangle = \mathrm{d}f(v)$ for every tangent vector $v$.

In coordinates, with $g^{ij}$ the entries of $g^{-1}$ and $|g| = \det g$:
$$
\nabla f = \sum_{i,j} g^{ij}\, \partial_j f\; \partial_i x, \qquad
\Delta f = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|g|}} \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \Big( \sqrt{|g|}\, g^{ij}\, \partial_j f \Big).
$$

The **divergence** of a tangent field is minus the adjoint of the gradient, and the **Laplace–Beltrami operator** is $\Delta = \operatorname{div} \nabla$. On a plane patch ($g = I$) it is the usual Laplacian $\partial_{11} + \partial_{22}$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.3 — Green's formula]{.tag} Let $S$ be a compact surface without boundary and $f, h$ smooth functions on it. Then
$$
\int_S f\, \Delta h \,\mathrm{d}A = - \int_S \langle \nabla f, \nabla h \rangle \,\mathrm{d}A .
$$

Consequently $-\Delta$ is symmetric and positive semi-definite for the $L^2$ inner product, and on a connected surface its kernel is the constant functions.

::: proof
The divergence theorem on a closed surface gives $\int_S \operatorname{div}(f \nabla h) = 0$. The product rule
$$
\operatorname{div}(f \nabla h) = \langle \nabla f, \nabla h \rangle + f\, \Delta h
$$
then gives the formula.

Taking $f = h$ shows that $-\int h \Delta h = \int \|\nabla h\|^2 \geq 0$. Equality forces $\nabla h = 0$, so $h$ is constant on each connected component. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

On a surface with boundary the formula gains a boundary term $\int_{\partial S} f\, \partial_\nu h$; it vanishes under Dirichlet ($f = 0$) or Neumann ($\partial_\nu h = 0$) conditions.

::: ex
[Example 0.4 — The round sphere]{.tag} On the unit sphere the eigenfunctions of $-\Delta$ are the spherical harmonics. The eigenvalue $\ell(\ell + 1)$ has multiplicity $2\ell + 1$, so the spectrum starts
$$
0,\ \ 2, 2, 2,\ \ 6 \ (\times 5),\ \ 12 \ (\times 7),\ \dots
$$

The three coordinate functions $x, y, z$ restricted to the sphere span the eigenspace of eigenvalue 2. This is the reference against which the discrete Laplacian of [ch. 1](#ch1) is tested.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.5 — Generalised symmetric eigenproblem]{.tag} Let $A$ be symmetric and $B$ symmetric positive definite, both $n \times n$. There is a basis $\phi_1, \dots, \phi_n$ and reals $\lambda_1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_n$ such that
$$
A \phi_k = \lambda_k B \phi_k, \qquad \phi_k^\top B \phi_l = \delta_{kl}.
$$

Moreover $\lambda_1$ is the minimum of the Rayleigh quotient $R(x) = x^\top A x / x^\top B x$, and $\lambda_k$ is its minimum on the $B$-orthogonal complement of $\phi_1, \dots, \phi_{k-1}$.

::: proof
Write $B = R^\top R$ (Cholesky) and set $y = R x$. The problem becomes the ordinary symmetric problem for $C = R^{-\top} A R^{-1}$.

The spectral theorem gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $y_k$ of $C$; the vectors $\phi_k = R^{-1} y_k$ are then $B$-orthonormal and solve the original problem.

The Rayleigh quotient of $x$ equals that of $y$ for $C$, which gives the variational characterisation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In practice $A$ and $B$ are large and sparse. Only the smallest eigenpairs are needed; they are computed by shift-invert Lanczos (`scipy.sparse.linalg.eigsh` with `sigma`). Linear systems with a sparse symmetric positive definite matrix are solved by a sparse Cholesky factorisation, computed once and reused.

::: ex
[Example 0.6 — Finite elements in one dimension]{.tag} Solve $-u'' = \lambda u$ on $[0, 1]$ with $u(0) = u(1) = 0$.

Write $u = \sum_i u_i \psi_i$ with the piecewise-linear “hat” functions $\psi_i$ of a grid of step $h$, and test the equation against each $\psi_j$. Integration by parts gives $K u = \lambda M u$ with
$$
K_{ij} = \int_0^1 \psi_i' \psi_j', \qquad M_{ij} = \int_0^1 \psi_i \psi_j .
$$

Here $K = \frac{1}{h}\,\mathrm{tridiag}(-1, 2, -1)$ and $M = \frac{h}{6}\,\mathrm{tridiag}(1, 4, 1)$. Replacing $M$ by the diagonal of its row sums, $h I$, is called **mass lumping**. The exact eigenvalues are $(k \pi)^2$.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import eigh

n = 50                                   # interior nodes on [0, 1], u(0) = u(1) = 0
h = 1.0 / (n + 1)
K = (np.diag(2 * np.ones(n)) - np.diag(np.ones(n - 1), 1) - np.diag(np.ones(n - 1), -1)) / h
M = h / 6 * (np.diag(4 * np.ones(n)) + np.diag(np.ones(n - 1), 1) + np.diag(np.ones(n - 1), -1))
lam_consistent = eigh(K, M, eigvals_only=True)[:4]
lam_lumped = eigh(K, h * np.eye(n), eigvals_only=True)[:4]
exact = (np.pi * np.arange(1, 5)) ** 2
print("exact     ", np.round(exact, 2))
print("consistent", np.round(lam_consistent, 2))
print("lumped    ", np.round(lam_lumped, 2))
```

The output is

```
exact      [  9.87  39.48  88.83 157.91]
consistent [  9.87  39.53  89.08 158.71]
lumped     [  9.87  39.43  88.57 157.12]
```

The consistent mass matrix overestimates the eigenvalues and the lumped one underestimates them; both converge at order $h^2$. The same construction on triangles gives the operators of [ch. 1](#ch1).
:::

::: def
[Definition 0.7 — Convolution and equivariance]{.tag} On $\mathbb{R}^n$ the convolution of a signal $f$ with a filter $a$ is
$$
(f * a)(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\, a(x - y) \,\mathrm{d}y .
$$

It is **equivariant** to translations: with $(\tau_v f)(x) = f(x - v)$, we have $(\tau_v f) * a = \tau_v (f * a)$. The Fourier transform diagonalises it, $\widehat{f * a} = \hat f \cdot \hat a$, and the complex exponentials are the eigenfunctions of the Laplacian.

A surface has no translations and no global Fourier basis. Two substitutes are developed later: filters that are functions of the Laplace–Beltrami operator ([ch. 2](#ch2)), and filters applied in local charts, which need parallel transport ([ch. 6](#ch6)).
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   The metric $g = J^\top J$ determines lengths, areas, gradients and the Laplace–Beltrami operator; such quantities are intrinsic.
-   Green's formula makes $-\Delta$ symmetric and positive semi-definite, with constants in its kernel.
-   $A\phi = \lambda B \phi$ with $B \succ 0$ has a $B$-orthonormal eigenbasis, characterised by Rayleigh quotients.
-   The finite element method turns $-\Delta u = \lambda u$ into $K u = \lambda M u$ with a stiffness and a mass matrix.
-   Convolution is the translation-equivariant linear operator; surfaces need other constructions.
:::

## 1. Triangle meshes and discrete differential operators {#ch1}

A scanned or modelled surface reaches the computer as a list of triangles. This chapter defines functions on such a mesh and derives, with the finite element method, the discrete gradient, divergence and Laplacian that the rest of the course uses.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Triangle mesh]{.tag} A **triangle mesh** is a pair $(V, F)$: vertex positions $x_1, \dots, x_n \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and a list $F$ of triangles, each an ordered triple of vertex indices. The edges $E$ are the unordered pairs of vertices that share a triangle.

The mesh is **manifold** when every edge lies in one or two triangles and the triangles around each vertex form a single fan, closed (interior vertex) or open (boundary vertex). It is **oriented** when two triangles sharing an edge traverse it in opposite directions; the normal of a triangle $(i, j, k)$ is then $(x_j - x_i) \times (x_k - x_i)$ normalised.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Euler characteristic and counts]{.tag} The **Euler characteristic** of a mesh is $\chi = |V| - |E| + |F|$; it is $2$ for a sphere and $0$ for a torus, whatever the triangulation. For a closed manifold mesh,
$$
2|E| = 3|F|, \qquad |F| = 2|V| - 2\chi, \qquad |E| = 3|V| - 3\chi .
$$

::: proof
Each triangle has three edges and each edge of a closed mesh lies in exactly two triangles, so $3|F| = 2|E|$. Substituting $|E| = \frac{3}{2}|F|$ in $\chi = |V| - |E| + |F|$ gives $|F| = 2|V| - 2\chi$, then $|E|$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

A large closed mesh has about twice as many triangles as vertices, and average degree close to 6.
::::

::: def
[Definition 1.3 — Hat functions and the mass matrix]{.tag} The **hat function** $\psi_i$ is the continuous function, linear on each triangle, with $\psi_i(x_j) = \delta_{ij}$. A function given by its vertex values $u \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is interpolated as $u = \sum_i u_i \psi_i$.

The **mass matrix** is $M_{ij} = \int \psi_i \psi_j \,\mathrm{d}A$. On a triangle of area $A$ its local block is $\frac{A}{12}(1 + \delta_{ij})$. The **lumped** mass matrix is diagonal, with $M_{ii}$ equal to one third of the area of the triangles around vertex $i$. Then
$$
\int_S u \, v \,\mathrm{d}A \approx u^\top M v, \qquad \int_S u \,\mathrm{d}A \approx \mathbf{1}^\top M u .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.4 — Gradient of a hat function]{.tag} In a triangle with vertices $i, j, k$ in counter-clockwise order, area $A$ and unit normal $n$, let $e_i = x_k - x_j$ be the edge opposite to $i$. Then $\nabla \psi_i$ is constant on the triangle and
$$
\nabla \psi_i = \frac{n \times e_i}{2A} .
$$

::: proof
$\psi_i$ is linear, vanishes on the edge $e_i$ and equals 1 at $x_i$. Its gradient is therefore orthogonal to $e_i$ within the plane of the triangle, pointing towards $x_i$, and of norm $1 / \text{height} = \|e_i\| / (2A)$.

The vector $n \times e_i$ has exactly this direction, since the interior lies to the left of a counter-clockwise edge, and norm $\|e_i\|$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 1.5 — Stiffness matrix (weak Laplacian)]{.tag} The **stiffness matrix** is
$$
L_{ij} = \int_S \langle \nabla \psi_i, \nabla \psi_j \rangle \,\mathrm{d}A ,
$$
so that $u^\top L u = \int_S \|\nabla u\|^2$ is the Dirichlet energy of the interpolated function.

Testing $-\Delta u = f$ against every $\psi_j$ and using Green's formula (Theorem 0.3) gives the discrete equation $L u = M f$. The pointwise discrete Laplacian is therefore $-M^{-1} L$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.6 — The cotangent formula]{.tag} For an interior edge $ij$, let $\alpha_{ij}$ and $\beta_{ij}$ be the two angles opposite to it in its two triangles (one angle for a boundary edge). Then
$$
L_{ij} = -\frac{1}{2} \big( \cot \alpha_{ij} + \cot \beta_{ij} \big), \qquad L_{ii} = - \sum_{j \neq i} L_{ij},
$$
and $L_{ij} = 0$ when $i \neq j$ are not joined by an edge.

::: proof
The integrand is constant on each triangle. In a triangle $(i, j, k)$ with angle $\theta_k$ at $k$, Proposition 1.4 gives
$$
A \,\langle \nabla \psi_i, \nabla \psi_j \rangle = \frac{\langle n \times e_i, n \times e_j \rangle}{4A} = \frac{\langle e_i, e_j \rangle}{4A}.
$$

The edges $e_i = x_k - x_j$ and $e_j = x_i - x_k$ meet at $x_k$, so $\langle e_i, e_j \rangle = -\|e_i\| \|e_j\| \cos \theta_k$. Since $2A = \|e_i\| \|e_j\| \sin \theta_k$, the contribution is $-\frac12 \cot \theta_k$.

Summing over the triangles containing the edge gives the off-diagonal entry. The hats sum to 1, so $\sum_j \nabla \psi_j = 0$ and each row of $L$ sums to zero. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — the cotangent Laplacian]{.tag}
$$
(L u)_i = \frac12 \sum_{j \sim i} \big( \cot \alpha_{ij} + \cot \beta_{ij} \big) (u_i - u_j), \qquad -\Delta u \approx M^{-1} L u
$$
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 1.7 — Properties of the cotangent Laplacian]{.tag}

-   **Symmetric and positive semi-definite**, because $u^\top L u = \int \|\nabla u\|^2 \geq 0$, for every mesh, even with obtuse angles.
-   **Constants in the kernel**, $L \mathbf{1} = 0$; on a connected mesh the kernel is exactly the constants.
-   **Local and sparse**: about 7 non-zeros per row.
-   **Positive weights** $\cot \alpha + \cot \beta \geq 0$ if and only if $\alpha_{ij} + \beta_{ij} \leq \pi$, the condition satisfied by an intrinsic Delaunay mesh. Only then is $L$ an M-matrix, which gives the discrete maximum principle used in [ch. 2](#ch2).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 1.8 — Gradient, divergence and the factorisation of $L$]{.tag} Let $G$ be the $3|F| \times n$ matrix that maps vertex values to the constant gradient on each triangle, and $\mathcal{A}$ the diagonal matrix of triangle areas, repeated three times. The **integrated divergence** of a field $X$, constant on each triangle, is the vector
$$
(\operatorname{div} X)_i = - \sum_{f \ni i} A_f \,\langle X_f, \nabla \psi_i|_f \rangle ,
$$
that is $\operatorname{div} = -G^\top \mathcal{A}$. Then
$$
L = G^\top \mathcal{A}\, G = -\operatorname{div} \circ \nabla .
$$

This mirrors Definition 0.2: the divergence is minus the adjoint of the gradient, now for the area-weighted inner products. The factorisation holds because each entry $L_{ij}$ is the area-weighted sum over triangles of $\langle \nabla \psi_i, \nabla \psi_j \rangle$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.9 — A regular grid recovers finite differences]{.tag} Triangulate the square grid of step $h$ by cutting each square along the same diagonal.

-   A diagonal edge faces two right angles, so its weight is $\frac12(\cot 90^\circ + \cot 90^\circ) = 0$.
-   A horizontal or vertical edge faces two angles of $45^\circ$, so its weight is $\frac12 (1 + 1) = 1$.
-   Each vertex lies in six triangles of area $h^2 / 2$, so its lumped mass is $h^2$.

Hence the discrete Laplacian at an interior vertex is
$$
-(M^{-1} L u)_{p,q} = \frac{u_{p+1,q} + u_{p-1,q} + u_{p,q+1} + u_{p,q-1} - 4 u_{p,q}}{h^2},
$$
the classical five-point stencil. Note that $L$ itself does not depend on $h$: the Dirichlet energy is invariant under scaling in 2D.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.10 — The spectrum of a triangulated sphere]{.tag} The code below triangulates 2000 nearly uniform points of the unit sphere (the convex hull of a Fibonacci lattice), assembles $L$ and the lumped $M$, and solves $L \phi = \lambda M \phi$ (Theorem 0.5).

```python
import numpy as np, scipy.sparse as sp
from scipy.sparse.linalg import eigsh
from scipy.spatial import ConvexHull

def sphere_mesh(n):
    """Fibonacci points on the unit sphere, triangulated by their convex hull."""
    i = np.arange(n) + 0.5
    phi, th = np.arccos(1 - 2 * i / n), np.pi * (1 + 5 ** 0.5) * i
    V = np.c_[np.cos(th) * np.sin(phi), np.sin(th) * np.sin(phi), np.cos(phi)]
    F = ConvexHull(V).simplices
    nrm = np.cross(V[F[:, 1]] - V[F[:, 0]], V[F[:, 2]] - V[F[:, 0]])
    flip = (nrm * V[F].sum(1)).sum(1) < 0          # orient every face outwards
    F[flip] = F[flip][:, ::-1]
    return V, F

def cotan_laplacian(V, F):
    """Stiffness matrix L (positive semi-definite) of Theorem 1.6."""
    I, J, W = [], [], []
    for k in range(3):
        i, j, o = F[:, k], F[:, (k + 1) % 3], F[:, (k + 2) % 3]
        u, v = V[i] - V[o], V[j] - V[o]               # the angle at o faces edge ij
        cot = (u * v).sum(1) / np.linalg.norm(np.cross(u, v), axis=1)
        I += [i, j]; J += [j, i]; W += [cot / 2, cot / 2]
    W = sp.csr_matrix((np.concatenate(W), (np.concatenate(I), np.concatenate(J))),
                      shape=(len(V), len(V)))
    return (sp.diags(np.asarray(W.sum(1)).ravel()) - W).tocsc()

def lumped_mass(V, F):
    area = 0.5 * np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V[F[:, 1]] - V[F[:, 0]], V[F[:, 2]] - V[F[:, 0]]), axis=1)
    return sp.diags(np.bincount(F.ravel(), np.repeat(area / 3, 3), len(V))).tocsc()

V, F = sphere_mesh(2000)
L, M = cotan_laplacian(V, F), lumped_mass(V, F)
print("faces:", len(F), " Euler characteristic:", len(V) - len(F) * 3 // 2 + len(F))
print("|L 1|_max =", abs(L @ np.ones(len(V))).max(), " area =", M.sum(), "(4 pi =", 4 * np.pi, ")")
lam = eigsh(L, k=16, M=M, sigma=-1e-6, which="LM")[0]
print(np.round(lam, 3))        # expected l(l+1): 0, 2 x3, 6 x5, 12 x7
```

It prints 3996 faces, $\chi = 2$, $\|L \mathbf{1}\|_\infty \approx 10^{-15}$, a total area of 12.547 (against $4\pi \approx 12.566$, the inscribed polyhedron is slightly smaller), and the spectrum
$$
0,\ \ 2.000\ (\times 3),\ \ 5.987\text{–}5.991\ (\times 5),\ \ 11.936\text{–}11.962\ (\times 7).
$$

The multiplicities of Example 0.4 are reproduced exactly, and the eigenvalues are within 0.6 %.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   A closed mesh has $|F| \approx 2|V|$ and average degree near 6.
-   Hat functions interpolate vertex values; the (lumped) mass matrix integrates them.
-   The stiffness matrix is the Dirichlet energy, with entries $-\frac12(\cot \alpha + \cot \beta)$.
-   $L$ is symmetric, positive semi-definite and sparse; positive weights need $\alpha + \beta \leq \pi$.
-   $L = G^\top \mathcal{A} G$ and $-\Delta \approx M^{-1} L$.
:::

## 2. Heat diffusion, geodesics and convolution on surfaces {#ch2}

Diffusing heat is the simplest process on a surface, and it encodes the geometry: the heat that reaches a point after a short time reveals its distance to the source. This chapter turns that remark into an algorithm for geodesic distances, and uses heat as the model of a convolution on a surface.

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Heat equation and heat kernel]{.tag} The **heat equation** on a closed surface is $\partial_t u = \Delta u$ with $u(\cdot, 0) = u_0$. With the eigenpairs $-\Delta \phi_k = \lambda_k \phi_k$, orthonormal in $L^2$, its solution is $u(x, t) = \int_S k_t(x, y)\, u_0(y) \,\mathrm{d}A(y)$, where the **heat kernel** is
$$
k_t(x, y) = \sum_{k \geq 0} e^{-\lambda_k t} \phi_k(x) \phi_k(y).
$$

The kernel is symmetric and positive, and it preserves the total heat: $\int_S k_t(x, y)\, \mathrm{d}A(y) = 1$. Only the metric enters, so it is intrinsic.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Discrete heat flow]{.tag} The backward Euler step of length $t$ for $M \dot u = -L u$ is
$$
(M + t L)\, u^{(1)} = M u^{(0)} .
$$

It is stable for every $t > 0$: the $M$-norm of $u$ does not increase. With the lumped (diagonal) $M$ and positive cotangent weights, $M + tL$ is an M-matrix, so a non-negative initial heat stays non-negative.

::: proof
Write $u = u^{(1)}$ and $u_0 = u^{(0)}$. Multiplying the step by $u^\top$ gives
$$
u^\top M u + t\, u^\top L u = u^\top M u_0 .
$$

The term $u^\top L u$ is non-negative (Proposition 1.7), and Cauchy–Schwarz for the $M$ inner product gives $\|u\|_M^2 \leq \|u\|_M \|u_0\|_M$.

For positivity, $M + tL$ has a positive diagonal and non-positive off-diagonal entries (the consistent mass matrix would add positive ones), and it is strictly diagonally dominant because the rows of $L$ sum to zero. Such a matrix has an entrywise non-negative inverse. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — Geodesic distance and the eikonal equation]{.tag} The **geodesic distance** $d(x, y)$ is the infimum of the lengths of the curves on $S$ from $x$ to $y$; a curve that realises it locally is a **geodesic**. The distance $\phi = d(x_0, \cdot)$ to a source solves the **eikonal equation**
$$
\|\nabla \phi\| = 1, \qquad \phi(x_0) = 0 ,
$$
in the viscosity sense: it is smooth away from $x_0$ and the cut locus, where several shortest paths meet.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 2.4 — Varadhan's formula (1967)]{.tag} On a compact Riemannian manifold, for points $x, y$,
$$
d(x, y) = \lim_{t \to 0} \sqrt{-4t \log k_t(x, y)} .
$$

The intuition is the Euclidean kernel $(4\pi t)^{-1} e^{-\|x - y\|^2 / 4t}$, whose logarithm is dominated by $-\|x - y\|^2 / 4t$ for small $t$. Varadhan (1967) proved the formula for heat equations with variable coefficients, which covers a metric written in local coordinates; the proof is beyond this course.
:::

Taking the formula literally is a bad algorithm: the logarithm amplifies the discretisation error of a tiny kernel. Crane, Weischedel and Wardetzky (2013) keep only the *direction* of the gradient of the heat, which is accurate, and recover the magnitude from the eikonal equation.

::: def
[Algorithm 2.5 — The heat method]{.tag} Given the source vertex $s$ and the mean edge length $h$:

1.  **Diffuse**: solve $(M + t L)\, u = M \delta_s$ with $t = h^2$ (Proposition 2.2).
2.  **Normalise**: on each triangle, set $X = -\nabla u / \|\nabla u\|$ (Proposition 1.4).
3.  **Integrate**: solve the Poisson equation $L \phi = G^\top \mathcal{A} X$ and shift $\phi$ so that $\phi_s = 0$.

Both matrices are fixed, so they are factorised once; each new source costs two solves with the stored factors (forward and back substitutions).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.6 — The Poisson step is a least-squares fit]{.tag} Among all functions $\phi$ (up to a constant), step 3 returns the minimiser of
$$
E(\phi) = \int_S \|\nabla \phi - X\|^2 \,\mathrm{d}A = (G\phi - X)^\top \mathcal{A}\, (G \phi - X).
$$

::: proof
$E$ is a convex quadratic. Its gradient is $2 G^\top \mathcal{A} (G \phi - X)$, and it vanishes exactly when $G^\top \mathcal{A} G \phi = G^\top \mathcal{A} X$, which is $L \phi = G^\top \mathcal{A} X$ by Proposition 1.8. The solution is unique up to the kernel of $L$, the constants. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Since $X$ has unit norm and points away from the source, the fitted $\phi$ is the function whose gradient best satisfies the eikonal equation with the right direction.
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.7 — Geodesics in heat on the sphere]{.tag} On the unit sphere the distance to a vertex $s$ is $\arccos \langle x, x_s \rangle$, which gives an exact reference. The gradients are computed per triangle with Proposition 1.4, and $L$ is assembled as $G^\top \mathcal{A} G$.

```python
import numpy as np, scipy.sparse as sp
from scipy.sparse.linalg import splu
from scipy.spatial import ConvexHull

def sphere_mesh(n):
    i = np.arange(n) + 0.5
    phi, th = np.arccos(1 - 2 * i / n), np.pi * (1 + 5 ** 0.5) * i
    V = np.c_[np.cos(th) * np.sin(phi), np.sin(th) * np.sin(phi), np.cos(phi)]
    F = ConvexHull(V).simplices
    nrm = np.cross(V[F[:, 1]] - V[F[:, 0]], V[F[:, 2]] - V[F[:, 0]])
    flip = (nrm * V[F].sum(1)).sum(1) < 0
    F[flip] = F[flip][:, ::-1]
    return V, F

def hat_gradients(V, F):
    """Per face: area, unit normal, and the gradients of the three hat functions."""
    N = np.cross(V[F[:, 1]] - V[F[:, 0]], V[F[:, 2]] - V[F[:, 0]])
    A = 0.5 * np.linalg.norm(N, axis=1); N = N / (2 * A[:, None])
    G = [np.cross(N, V[F[:, (k + 2) % 3]] - V[F[:, (k + 1) % 3]]) / (2 * A[:, None]) for k in range(3)]
    return A, N, G

def heat_geodesic(V, F, src, c=1.0):
    n = len(V)
    A, N, G = hat_gradients(V, F)
    rows = np.concatenate([F[:, a] for a in range(3) for b in range(3)])
    cols = np.concatenate([F[:, b] for a in range(3) for b in range(3)])
    vals = np.concatenate([A * (G[a] * G[b]).sum(1) for a in range(3) for b in range(3)])
    L = sp.csc_matrix((vals, (rows, cols)), shape=(n, n))         # stiffness = cotan matrix
    M = sp.diags(np.bincount(F.ravel(), np.repeat(A / 3, 3), n)).tocsc()
    h = np.linalg.norm(V[F[:, 0]] - V[F[:, 1]], axis=1).mean()
    u0 = np.zeros(n); u0[src] = 1.0
    u = splu((M + c * h ** 2 * L).tocsc()).solve(M @ u0)           # step 1: heat flow
    gu = sum(u[F[:, k], None] * G[k] for k in range(3))
    X = -gu / np.linalg.norm(gu, axis=1, keepdims=True)              # step 2: normalise
    b = np.zeros(n)
    for k in range(3):                                                # step 3: Poisson
        np.add.at(b, F[:, k], A * (X * G[k]).sum(1))
    phi = splu((L + 1e-10 * sp.eye(n)).tocsc()).solve(b)
    return phi - phi[src]

V, F = sphere_mesh(4000)
src = 0
exact = np.arccos(np.clip(V @ V[src], -1, 1))
for c in [0.1, 1.0, 10.0]:
    d = heat_geodesic(V, F, src, c)
    print(f"t = {c:4} h^2: mean |error| = {np.abs(d - exact).mean():.4f}, "
          f"max = {np.abs(d - exact).max():.4f} (diameter pi)")
```

The mean errors are 0.106, 0.025 and 0.010 for $t = 0.1 h^2$, $h^2$ and $10 h^2$, against a diameter of $\pi$.

A too small $t$ leaves the heat on a few vertices and the gradient directions are noisy. On the round sphere every $t$ gives the exact direction field by symmetry, so a larger $t$ only averages the noise; on a general surface a large $t$ smooths the distance and rounds its corners (Exercise 8).
:::

The heat kernel acts on a function like a Gaussian blur of width about $\sqrt{2t}$. This suggests what a convolution on a surface can be.

::: def
[Definition 2.8 — Spectral filters as convolutions]{.tag} For a function $g : [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}$, the **filter** $g(-\Delta)$ acts on $f$ through its spectral coefficients $\hat f_k = \langle f, \phi_k \rangle$:
$$
g(-\Delta) f = \sum_{k} g(\lambda_k)\, \hat f_k\, \phi_k .
$$

On $\mathbb{R}^n$ this is exactly the convolution with the filter of Fourier transform $g(\|\xi\|^2)$, radial by construction. The heat flow is $g(\lambda) = e^{-t\lambda}$.

Discretely, with the $M$-orthonormal eigenvectors $\Phi$ of $L$:
$$
g(-\Delta) f \approx \Phi\, g(\Lambda)\, \Phi^\top M f .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.9 — Filters commute with isometries]{.tag} Let $T : S \to S'$ be an isometry and $T^* f = f \circ T$. Then $T^* \circ g(-\Delta') = g(-\Delta) \circ T^*$. In particular the filter does not depend on the choice of eigenbasis inside an eigenspace.

::: proof
An isometry preserves the metric, hence the Laplace–Beltrami operator: $\Delta (f \circ T) = (\Delta' f) \circ T$. So $T^*$ maps each eigenspace of $\Delta'$ onto the eigenspace of $\Delta$ with the same eigenvalue, and $g(-\Delta)$ multiplies each eigenspace by $g(\lambda)$, whatever basis is chosen in it. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The price is isotropy: a function of $\Delta$ cannot tell directions apart. Directional filters need local charts and parallel transport ([ch. 6](#ch6)).
::::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   The heat kernel is intrinsic, positive and mass-preserving.
-   Backward Euler $(M + tL) u = M u_0$ is stable, and positive when the weights are.
-   Varadhan: $d^2 \approx -4t \log k_t$; the heat method keeps the gradient direction, then solves a Poisson equation.
-   With $t = h^2$ and prefactored matrices, a new source costs two cheap solves.
-   Functions of the Laplacian are isotropic convolutions and commute with isometries.
:::

## 3. Spectral geometry, curvature and spectral signatures {#ch3}

Laplacian eigenfunctions are the Fourier basis of a surface, and curvature measures how it departs from a plane. This chapter computes both and combines them into descriptors that survive bending.

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Manifold harmonics]{.tag} The **manifold harmonics** of a mesh are the solutions of
$$
L \phi_k = \lambda_k M \phi_k, \qquad \Phi^\top M \Phi = I, \qquad 0 = \lambda_0 \leq \lambda_1 \leq \dots
$$
(Theorem 0.5). The **spectral coefficients** of a function $f$ are $\hat f = \Phi^\top M f$, and the truncation to the first $k$ harmonics is $f_k = \Phi_k \Phi_k^\top M f$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Energy and low-pass filtering]{.tag} For $f = \Phi \hat f$,
$$
\|f\|_M^2 = \sum_k \hat f_k^2, \qquad f^\top L f = \sum_k \lambda_k \hat f_k^2 .
$$

The truncation $f_k$ is the $M$-orthogonal projection of $f$ on the span of the $k$ smoothest harmonics, and $\phi_k$ minimises the Dirichlet energy among unit functions orthogonal to $\phi_0, \dots, \phi_{k-1}$.

::: proof
Substitute $f = \Phi \hat f$ and use $\Phi^\top M \Phi = I$ and $\Phi^\top L \Phi = \Lambda$. The projection claim is the Pythagorean theorem in the $M$ inner product; the variational claim is Theorem 0.5. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 3.3 — The spectrum as a shape signature]{.tag} Isometric surfaces have the same Laplace–Beltrami spectrum, because an isometry preserves $\Delta$ (proof of Proposition 2.9). Reuter, Wolter and Peinecke (2006) use the first eigenvalues, normalised by the area, as a **Shape-DNA** to compare shapes up to isometry and scale.

The converse fails: Gordon, Webb and Wolpert (1992) built planar domains that are isospectral without being isometric. The spectrum is a strong but incomplete signature.
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.4 — Smoothing a shape by its spectrum]{.tag} Filter the three coordinate functions of a mesh: $V_k = \Phi_k \Phi_k^\top M V$. On a sphere, $V_4$ is already the sphere, since $x, y, z$ lie in the first eigenspaces (Example 0.4). On the prolate spheroid of Code 3.12 (semi-axes 2, 1, 1) the mean vertex displacement $\|x - x_k\|$ is
$$
1.380\ (k = 1), \qquad 0.125\ (k = 4), \qquad 0.028\ (k = 16), \qquad 0.0012\ (k = 80).
$$

With $k = 1$ every vertex collapses to the centroid. A few dozen harmonics keep the overall shape and drop the fine detail; editing the low coefficients deforms a shape smoothly.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.5 — Curvatures]{.tag} The **shape operator** at $p$ is the derivative of the unit normal, $\mathrm{d}n_p : T_p S \to T_p S$, a symmetric map. Its eigenvalues are the **principal curvatures** $\kappa_1, \kappa_2$. The **mean curvature** is $H = (\kappa_1 + \kappa_2)/2$ and the **Gaussian curvature** is $K = \kappa_1 \kappa_2$.

For the unit sphere with outward normal, $\kappa_1 = \kappa_2 = 1$. By Gauss's Theorema Egregium, $K$ is intrinsic, while $H$ depends on the embedding: a rolled sheet has $K = 0$ and $H \neq 0$.
:::

On a smooth surface the coordinate map $x$ satisfies $\Delta x = -2H n$. The discrete counterpart is an exact statement about areas.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.6 — Mean curvature as the gradient of area]{.tag} Let $\mathcal{A}(V)$ be the total area of a mesh with vertex positions $V$ (an $n \times 3$ matrix). Then for every vertex $i$
$$
\nabla_{x_i} \mathcal{A} = (L V)_i ,
$$
and $(M^{-1} L V)_i \approx 2 H n_i$ is the discrete mean curvature normal.

::: proof
In one triangle, moving $x_i$ changes the area through the height over the opposite edge $e_i$ only. The gradient is $\frac12 n \times e_i$, which equals $A \,\nabla \psi_i$ by Proposition 1.4.

On the other hand,
$$
(LV)_i = \sum_f A_f \sum_j \langle \nabla \psi_i, \nabla \psi_j \rangle\, x_j .
$$

On a triangle, $\sum_j x_j \nabla \psi_j^\top$ is the gradient of the identity map, the orthogonal projector $P_f$ on the plane of the triangle, and $P_f \nabla \psi_i = \nabla \psi_i$.

Hence
$$
(L V)_i = \sum_{f \ni i} A_f\, \nabla \psi_i|_f = \sum_{f \ni i} \nabla_{x_i} A_f .
$$

[∎]{.qed}
:::

Moving every vertex against this gradient decreases the area fastest: it is the discrete **mean curvature flow**, used for smoothing (Desbrun et al., 1999).
::::

::: def
[Definition 3.7 — Angle defect]{.tag} At an interior vertex $i$ with triangle angles $\theta_i^f$, the **angle defect** is
$$
K_i = 2\pi - \sum_{f \ni i} \theta_i^f .
$$

It is zero when the triangles around $i$ unfold flat into the plane. Divided by the vertex area $M_{ii}$, it estimates the Gaussian curvature.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.8 — Discrete Gauss–Bonnet]{.tag} For a closed manifold triangle mesh,
$$
\sum_{i} K_i = 2\pi \chi .
$$

::: proof
The angles of a triangle sum to $\pi$, so $\sum_i K_i = 2\pi |V| - \pi |F|$. By Proposition 1.2, $|F| = 2|E| - 2|F|$, hence
$$
2\pi |V| - \pi |F| = 2\pi |V| - 2\pi |E| + 2\pi |F| = 2\pi \chi .
$$

[∎]{.qed}
:::

The smooth theorem $\int_S K \,\mathrm{d}A = 2\pi \chi$ says the same: the total curvature is fixed by the topology, whatever the geometry.
::::

::: def
[Definition 3.9 — Heat kernel signature (HKS)]{.tag} Sun, Ovsjanikov and Guibas (2009) define, for each point and time,
$$
\mathrm{HKS}(x, t) = k_t(x, x) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t} \phi_k(x)^2 .
$$

It is intrinsic, hence invariant to isometries, and multiscale: small $t$ sees the neighbourhood, large $t$ the whole shape. For small $t$,
$$
\mathrm{HKS}(x, t) = \frac{1}{4\pi t} + \frac{K(x)}{12 \pi} + O(t).
$$

If the eigenvalues are simple, a homeomorphism that preserves the HKS for all $t$ is an isometry (Sun et al., 2009): the signature is informative.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.10 — Wave kernel signature (WKS)]{.tag} Aubry, Schlickewei and Cremers (2011) replace the low-pass weights $e^{-\lambda t}$ by band-pass weights centred at the log-energy $e$:
$$
\mathrm{WKS}(x, e) = \frac{\sum_k \phi_k(x)^2\, w_e(\lambda_k)}{\sum_k w_e(\lambda_k)}, \qquad w_e(\lambda) = \exp\Big( -\frac{(e - \log \lambda)^2}{2\sigma^2} \Big).
$$

Each energy selects a band of frequencies, so the WKS separates scales better and locates points more precisely.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.11 — Global point signature (GPS)]{.tag} Rustamov (2007) embeds each point in a sequence space:
$$
\mathrm{GPS}(x) = \Big( \frac{\phi_1(x)}{\sqrt{\lambda_1}}, \frac{\phi_2(x)}{\sqrt{\lambda_2}}, \dots \Big).
$$

Squared distances in this embedding are $G(x, x) + G(y, y) - 2G(x, y)$, with $G$ the Green's function of $-\Delta$. The GPS depends on the signs of the eigenfunctions, so it serves for shape-level statistics such as histograms of distances.
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.12 — Curvature and signatures of a spheroid]{.tag} For the prolate spheroid with semi-axes 2, 1, 1, the exact values are $K = 4$, $H = 2$ at the tips and $K = 0.25$, $H = 0.625$ on the equator.

```python
import numpy as np, scipy.sparse as sp
from scipy.sparse.linalg import eigsh
from scipy.spatial import ConvexHull

def sphere_mesh(n):
    i = np.arange(n) + 0.5
    phi, th = np.arccos(1 - 2 * i / n), np.pi * (1 + 5 ** 0.5) * i
    V = np.c_[np.cos(th) * np.sin(phi), np.sin(th) * np.sin(phi), np.cos(phi)]
    F = ConvexHull(V).simplices
    nrm = np.cross(V[F[:, 1]] - V[F[:, 0]], V[F[:, 2]] - V[F[:, 0]])
    flip = (nrm * V[F].sum(1)).sum(1) < 0
    F[flip] = F[flip][:, ::-1]
    return V, F

def operators(V, F):
    """Cotan stiffness L, lumped mass M, and the angle defect at each vertex."""
    n = len(V); I, J, W = [], [], []; angle_sum = np.zeros(n)
    for k in range(3):
        i, j, o = F[:, k], F[:, (k + 1) % 3], F[:, (k + 2) % 3]
        u, v = V[i] - V[o], V[j] - V[o]
        cos_, sin_ = (u * v).sum(1), np.linalg.norm(np.cross(u, v), axis=1)
        I += [i, j]; J += [j, i]; W += [cos_ / sin_ / 2] * 2
        np.add.at(angle_sum, o, np.arctan2(sin_, cos_))       # interior angle at o
    W = sp.csr_matrix((np.concatenate(W), (np.concatenate(I), np.concatenate(J))), shape=(n, n))
    L = (sp.diags(np.asarray(W.sum(1)).ravel()) - W).tocsc()
    area = 0.5 * np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V[F[:, 1]] - V[F[:, 0]], V[F[:, 2]] - V[F[:, 0]]), axis=1)
    mass = np.bincount(F.ravel(), np.repeat(area / 3, 3), n)
    return L, sp.diags(mass).tocsc(), mass, 2 * np.pi - angle_sum

V, F = sphere_mesh(2000)
V = V * np.array([2.0, 1.0, 1.0])                         # prolate spheroid, semi-axes 2, 1, 1
L, M, mass, defect = operators(V, F)
K = defect / mass                                          # Gaussian curvature per unit area
H = np.linalg.norm((L @ V) / mass[:, None], axis=1) / 2   # |Delta x| / 2 = |H|
tip, eq = np.argmax(V[:, 0]), np.argmin(np.abs(V[:, 0]) + np.abs(V[:, 2]))
print(f"sum of angle defects = {defect.sum():.6f}   (2 pi chi = {4 * np.pi:.6f})")
print(f"tip:     K = {K[tip]:.2f} (exact 4),    H = {H[tip]:.2f} (exact 2)")
print(f"equator: K = {K[eq]:.2f} (exact 0.25), H = {H[eq]:.3f} (exact 0.625)")

lam, phi = eigsh(L, k=80, M=M, sigma=-1e-6, which="LM")
for t in [0.1, 1.0]:
    hks = (np.exp(-lam * t) * phi ** 2).sum(1)              # Definition 3.9
    print(f"HKS(t = {t}): tip {hks[tip]:.3f}, equator {hks[eq]:.3f};",
          f"1/(4 pi t) + K/(12 pi): {1 / (4 * np.pi * t) + 4 / (12 * np.pi):.3f},",
          f"{1 / (4 * np.pi * t) + 0.25 / (12 * np.pi):.3f}")
for k in [1, 4, 16, 80]:                                     # Example 3.4: spectral smoothing
    Vk = phi[:, :k] @ (phi[:, :k].T @ (mass[:, None] * V))
    print(f"k = {k:2d}: mean |x - x_k| = {np.linalg.norm(V - Vk, axis=1).mean():.4f}")
```

The sum of the angle defects is $12.566371 = 4\pi$ to all printed digits, as Theorem 3.8 predicts. The mesh gives $K = 3.94$ and $H = 1.98$ at the tip, and $K = 0.25$, $H = 0.625$ on the equator.

At $t = 0.1$ the HKS is 0.880 at the tip and 0.807 on the equator, close to the asymptotic values 0.902 and 0.802: the more curved tip keeps more heat. At $t = 1$ the expansion no longer applies (0.125 against 0.186).
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Manifold harmonics solve $L\phi = \lambda M \phi$ and give spectral coefficients and filters.
-   Isometric shapes share their spectrum, a strong but incomplete signature.
-   The area gradient is $LV$, so $M^{-1} L V \approx 2Hn$; angle defects give $K$.
-   Discrete Gauss–Bonnet: $\sum_i K_i = 2\pi\chi$ exactly.
-   HKS, WKS and GPS are isometry-invariant point signatures.
:::

## 4. Deformation, parameterization and topology {#ch4}

Editing a shape and flattening it onto the plane both minimise geometric energies built from the operators of [ch. 1](#ch1). Topology decides what flattening can achieve.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Geometric energies and Laplacian editing]{.tag} A **geometric energy** is a function of the vertex positions that measures a deviation: the Dirichlet energy $\operatorname{tr}(V^\top L V)$ (Proposition 1.8), the area (Theorem 3.6), or the change of a rest shape. Deformation fixes some **handle** vertices at targets $c_i$ and minimises an energy over the others.

**Laplacian editing** (Sorkine et al., 2004) keeps the differential coordinates $\delta = L V$ of the rest shape:
$$
\min_{V'} \ \|L V' - \delta\|^2 + w \sum_{i \in \text{handles}} \|x'_i - c_i\|^2 .
$$

It is a linear least-squares problem. In this basic form $\delta$ does not rotate: a handle turned by 90° shears the surface details instead of turning them. Sorkine et al. add linearised local transformations; ARAP treats rotations exactly.
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.2 — As-rigid-as-possible energy]{.tag} Sorkine and Alexa (2007) let every vertex carry its own rotation $R_i \in SO(3)$ and penalise the deviation of each edge vector $e_{ij} = x_i - x_j$ from a rotated copy:
$$
E(V', R) = \sum_i \sum_{j \sim i} w_{ij}\, \big\| e'_{ij} - R_i\, e_{ij} \big\|^2 ,
$$
with the cotangent weights $w_{ij}$ of Theorem 1.6. A rigid motion of the whole shape costs nothing.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.3 — The local step is an orthogonal Procrustes problem]{.tag} For fixed $V'$, let $S_i = \sum_{j \sim i} w_{ij}\, e_{ij} e'^{\top}_{ij}$ with singular value decomposition $S_i = U \Sigma W^\top$. The minimising rotation is
$$
R_i = W D U^\top, \qquad D = \mathrm{diag}\big(1, 1, \det(W U^\top)\big).
$$

::: proof
Expanding the squares, the terms of $E$ that depend on $R_i$ are
$$
-2 \sum_j w_{ij}\, e'^\top_{ij} R_i e_{ij} = -2 \operatorname{tr}(R_i S_i).
$$

So $R_i$ maximises $\operatorname{tr}(R S_i) = \operatorname{tr}(Z \Sigma)$ with $Z = W^\top R U$ orthogonal.

Since $|Z_{kk}| \leq 1$, $\operatorname{tr}(Z\Sigma) \leq \sum_k \sigma_k$, with equality at $Z = I$, that is $R = W U^\top$.

If this matrix is a reflection, the best $Z$ with determinant $-1$ flips the sign attached to the smallest singular value, which gives $D$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 4.4 — Local–global iterations]{.tag} For fixed rotations, $E$ is quadratic in $V'$ and its minimiser solves
$$
L V' = b, \qquad b_i = \sum_{j \sim i} \frac{w_{ij}}{2}\, (R_i + R_j)\, e_{ij},
$$
restricted to the free vertices. Alternating the local step (Theorem 4.3) and this global step never increases $E$.

Each step minimises $E$ exactly over one block of variables, so the energy decreases monotonically: block coordinate descent. The matrix $L$ does not change, so its Cholesky factor is computed once.
:::

Flattening asks how much distortion is unavoidable; topology answers part of the question.

::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — Topological constraints]{.tag} Closed orientable surfaces are classified, up to homeomorphism, by their **genus** $g$ (the number of handles), and $\chi = 2 - 2g$. The Gauss–Bonnet theorem $\int_S K = 2\pi\chi$ (smooth form of Theorem 3.8) and topology then imply:

-   A closed surface with a flat metric ($K \equiv 0$) has $\chi = 0$: among closed orientable surfaces, only the torus can be flat.
-   No closed surface maps injectively and continuously into the plane (invariance of domain), so a sphere-like surface must be cut before flattening. A disk-like patch can be flattened, at the price of distortion when $K \neq 0$.
-   A flattening that is flat everywhere except at a few **cone points** concentrates the curvature there; their angle defects sum to $2\pi\chi$.
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.6 — Parameterization and distortion]{.tag} A **parameterization** of a disk-like mesh is a piecewise-linear map $u$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$, given by vertex positions $u_i$. On each triangle its Jacobian $J_f$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, in a local frame of the triangle, with singular values $\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2$. The map is

-   **isometric** if $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = 1$ (lengths kept),
-   **conformal** if $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2$ (angles kept),
-   **equiareal** if $\sigma_1 \sigma_2 = 1$ (areas kept),

and **valid** if $\det J_f > 0$ on every triangle (no flip). Isometric is conformal plus equiareal; by the Theorema Egregium it requires $K = 0$.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 4.7 — Tutte (1963), Floater (1997)]{.tag} Let a disk-like mesh have its boundary vertices mapped, in order, onto a strictly convex polygon. Put every interior vertex at a convex combination of its neighbours:
$$
u_i = \sum_{j \sim i} \lambda_{ij}\, u_j, \qquad \lambda_{ij} > 0, \quad \sum_{j} \lambda_{ij} = 1 .
$$

Then this linear system has a unique solution, and the resulting map is a valid parameterization: a bijection onto the polygon with no flipped or degenerate triangle.

*Proof sketch.* The system matrix is a weakly diagonally dominant M-matrix, connected to the fixed boundary, hence invertible. Any linear function of $u$ satisfies a discrete maximum principle, so every interior vertex lies strictly inside the polygon. Injectivity follows by counting the angles around vertices; see Floater (2003) for the complete argument, which also covers merely convex polygons when no interior edge joins two boundary vertices.
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.8 — Harmonic and conformal parameterizations]{.tag} With $\lambda_{ij}$ proportional to the cotangent weights, $u$ minimises the Dirichlet energy $\operatorname{tr}(U^\top L U)$ with the boundary fixed: a **harmonic** map. It is closer to conformal, but negative weights (obtuse triangles) can break the guarantee of Theorem 4.7; Floater's mean-value weights are positive and stay close to it.

**Least-squares conformal maps** (Lévy et al., 2002) free the boundary. They minimise the violation of the Cauchy–Riemann equations, $\sum_f A_f \|\nabla v - n \times \nabla u\|^2$, with two vertices pinned to remove similarities.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.9 — Tutte versus harmonic flattening]{.tag} A sphere minus a polar cap is a disk. Its boundary is pinned to the unit circle and Theorem 4.7 is solved with uniform (Tutte) and cotangent (harmonic) weights. The code counts flips and averages $\sigma_1 / \sigma_2$, equal to 1 for a conformal map.

```python
import numpy as np, scipy.sparse as sp
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve
from scipy.spatial import ConvexHull

def sphere_mesh(n):
    i = np.arange(n) + 0.5
    phi, th = np.arccos(1 - 2 * i / n), np.pi * (1 + 5 ** 0.5) * i
    V = np.c_[np.cos(th) * np.sin(phi), np.sin(th) * np.sin(phi), np.cos(phi)]
    F = ConvexHull(V).simplices
    nrm = np.cross(V[F[:, 1]] - V[F[:, 0]], V[F[:, 2]] - V[F[:, 0]])
    flip = (nrm * V[F].sum(1)).sum(1) < 0
    F[flip] = F[flip][:, ::-1]
    return V, F

V, F = sphere_mesh(1500)
F = F[(V[F, 2] > -0.3).all(1)]                       # a disk: the sphere minus a polar cap
used = np.unique(F); remap = -np.ones(len(V), int); remap[used] = np.arange(len(used))
V, F = V[used], remap[F]
n = len(V)

# boundary edges appear in a single face; chain them into a loop
E = np.concatenate([F[:, [0, 1]], F[:, [1, 2]], F[:, [2, 0]]])
key = {tuple(e) for e in E}
nxt = {a: b for a, b in E if (b, a) not in key}
loop = [next(iter(nxt))]
while nxt[loop[-1]] != loop[0]:
    loop.append(nxt[loop[-1]])
seg = np.linalg.norm(V[loop] - V[np.roll(loop, -1)], axis=1)
ang = 2 * np.pi * np.r_[0, np.cumsum(seg)[:-1]] / seg.sum()
U_b = np.c_[np.cos(ang), np.sin(ang)]                 # boundary pinned to the unit circle

def weights(kind):
    I, J, W = [], [], []
    for k in range(3):
        i, j, o = F[:, k], F[:, (k + 1) % 3], F[:, (k + 2) % 3]
        u, v = V[i] - V[o], V[j] - V[o]
        w = np.ones(len(F)) if kind == "uniform" else \
            (u * v).sum(1) / np.linalg.norm(np.cross(u, v), axis=1) / 2
        I += [i, j]; J += [j, i]; W += [w, w]
    Wm = sp.csr_matrix((np.concatenate(W), (np.concatenate(I), np.concatenate(J))), shape=(n, n))
    if kind == "uniform":
        Wm.data[:] = 1.0                              # each edge counted once
    return (sp.diags(np.asarray(Wm.sum(1)).ravel()) - Wm).tocsr()

inner = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(n), loop)
for kind in ["uniform", "cotan"]:
    L = weights(kind)
    U = np.zeros((n, 2)); U[loop] = U_b
    rhs = -L[inner][:, loop] @ U_b
    U[inner] = np.c_[spsolve(L[inner][:, inner].tocsc(), rhs[:, 0]),
                     spsolve(L[inner][:, inner].tocsc(), rhs[:, 1])]
    e1, e2 = U[F[:, 1]] - U[F[:, 0]], U[F[:, 2]] - U[F[:, 0]]
    signed = 0.5 * (e1[:, 0] * e2[:, 1] - e1[:, 1] * e2[:, 0])
    p1, p2 = V[F[:, 1]] - V[F[:, 0]], V[F[:, 2]] - V[F[:, 0]]
    x = p1 / np.linalg.norm(p1, axis=1, keepdims=True)           # local frame of each 3D face
    y = p2 - (p2 * x).sum(1, keepdims=True) * x; y /= np.linalg.norm(y, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    P = np.stack([np.c_[(p1 * x).sum(1), (p1 * y).sum(1)], np.c_[(p2 * x).sum(1), (p2 * y).sum(1)]], 2)
    Q = np.stack([e1, e2], 2)                                      # columns = 2D edges
    s = np.linalg.svd(Q @ np.linalg.inv(P), compute_uv=False)      # singular values of the Jacobian
    print(f"{kind:8s}: flipped = {(signed <= 0).sum()}, mean sigma1/sigma2 = {(s[:, 0] / s[:, 1]).mean():.3f}")
```

Neither map flips a triangle. The mean ratio $\sigma_1/\sigma_2$ is 1.560 for Tutte's weights and 1.120 for the cotangent weights: the harmonic map is much closer to conformal.
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.10 — Toric covers (Maron et al., 2017)]{.tag} CNNs need a flat domain with translations, and only the torus is a flat closed surface (Proposition 4.5). Maron et al. (2017) therefore map a sphere-like surface to a torus:

-   choose a triplet of points on the surface;
-   glue four copies of the surface, cut along paths through the three points, into a torus: a fourfold cover of the surface, branched at the triplet;
-   map this torus conformally onto a flat square torus, which becomes an image with periodic boundaries.

Why a torus: the Riemann–Hurwitz formula gives $\chi(T) = 4\chi(S) - r$, where $r$ sums $e - 1$ over the preimages of index $e$ of the branch points. One preimage of index 4 over each of two points, and two of index 2 over the third, give $r = 3 + 3 + 2$, so $\chi(T) = 8 - 8 = 0$.

A standard CNN with cyclic padding convolves this image without seams. Several triplets give several images, and per-pixel predictions such as segmentation labels are pulled back to the surface and aggregated.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   Laplacian editing keeps differential coordinates without rotating them; ARAP adds a rotation per vertex.
-   ARAP alternates a Procrustes SVD step and a prefactored solve with $L$; the energy decreases.
-   $\chi = 2 - 2g$ and Gauss–Bonnet: only the torus can be flat, so closed surfaces are cut or covered.
-   Tutte's map of a disk is always valid; cotangent weights are closer to conformal; LSCM frees the boundary.
-   Toric covers map a sphere-like surface to a flat torus, where an ordinary CNN applies.
:::

## 5. Maps between surfaces and shape matching {#ch5}

Matching two shapes means finding, for each point of one, the corresponding point of the other: the same fingertip on a body in two poses. A point-to-point map is a hard combinatorial object; this chapter replaces it with a small matrix acting on functions, computed by linear algebra.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Pointwise maps and pullbacks]{.tag} A **pointwise map** $T : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{N}$ between meshes with $n_\mathcal{M}$ and $n_\mathcal{N}$ vertices sends each vertex of $\mathcal{M}$ to a vertex of $\mathcal{N}$. It is stored as a binary matrix $\Pi \in \{0, 1\}^{n_\mathcal{M} \times n_\mathcal{N}}$ with one 1 per row.

Its **pullback** transports functions backwards, $T^F g = g \circ T$, and in matrix form $T^F g = \Pi g$. The pullback is linear even when $T$ is not smooth: this is the starting point of functional maps.
:::

::: def
[Definition 5.2 — Functional map (Ovsjanikov et al., 2012)]{.tag} Let $\Phi_\mathcal{M}$ and $\Phi_\mathcal{N}$ hold the first $k$ manifold harmonics of each shape (Definition 3.1). The **functional map** of $T$ is the $k \times k$ matrix
$$
C = \Phi_\mathcal{M}^\top M_\mathcal{M}\, \Pi\, \Phi_\mathcal{N} .
$$

A function with coefficients $a$ on $\mathcal{N}$ is sent to the function with coefficients $C a$ on $\mathcal{M}$. A map between thousands of vertices becomes a matrix of a few hundred entries, and near-isometric maps have a $C$ concentrated near the diagonal (Theorem 5.3).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.3 — Isometries give structured functional maps]{.tag} Let $T$ be an isometry between smooth surfaces and use complete eigenbases. Then $C$ is orthogonal and commutes with the Laplacians:
$$
C\, \Lambda_\mathcal{N} = \Lambda_\mathcal{M}\, C, \qquad C^\top C = I .
$$

::: proof
An isometry preserves the Laplace–Beltrami operator:
$$
\Delta_\mathcal{M}(g \circ T) = (\Delta_\mathcal{N} g) \circ T, \qquad \text{so} \qquad T^F \Delta_\mathcal{N} = \Delta_\mathcal{M} T^F .
$$

Writing this identity in the two eigenbases gives $C \Lambda_\mathcal{N} = \Lambda_\mathcal{M} C$.

An isometry also preserves areas, so pullback preserves inner products:
$$
\langle g \circ T, h \circ T \rangle_\mathcal{M} = \langle g, h \rangle_\mathcal{N} .
$$

In orthonormal bases this reads $C^\top C = I$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Entry by entry, commutation says
$$
c_{ij}\, (\lambda^\mathcal{N}_j - \lambda^\mathcal{M}_i) = 0 :
$$
$C$ only mixes eigenfunctions of equal eigenvalue. With simple eigenvalues it is diagonal with entries $\pm 1$ (Exercise 9).
::::

::: def
[Definition 5.4 — Descriptor preservation]{.tag} Let $D_\mathcal{N}$ and $D_\mathcal{M}$ hold $q$ point descriptors per vertex, such as the WKS at $q$ energies (Definition 3.10), with $D_\mathcal{M} \approx \Pi D_\mathcal{N}$ when $T$ is an isometry.

In spectral coefficients, $G = \Phi^\top M D$, preservation reads
$$
C\, G_\mathcal{N} = G_\mathcal{M} .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.5 — Computing $C$ row by row]{.tag} The problem
$$
\min_C\ \|C G_\mathcal{N} - G_\mathcal{M}\|_F^2 + \alpha\, \|C \Lambda_\mathcal{N} - \Lambda_\mathcal{M} C\|_F^2
$$
separates over the rows of $C$. Row $c_i$ solves the $k \times k$ system
$$
\big( G_\mathcal{N} G_\mathcal{N}^\top + \alpha\, \mathrm{diag}_j (\lambda^\mathcal{M}_i - \lambda^\mathcal{N}_j)^2 \big)\, c_i^\top = G_\mathcal{N}\, (G_\mathcal{M})_i^\top .
$$

::: proof
Both Frobenius norms are sums over rows. Row $i$ of the first residual is $c_i G_\mathcal{N} - (G_\mathcal{M})_i$, and entry $(i, j)$ of the commutator is
$$
c_{ij}\, (\lambda^\mathcal{N}_j - \lambda^\mathcal{M}_i).
$$

The cost of row $i$ is a convex quadratic in $c_i$, whose normal equations are the stated system. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.6 — From a functional map back to points]{.tag} If $\Pi \Phi_\mathcal{N} = \Phi_\mathcal{M} C$ held exactly, row $x$ would read $\Phi_\mathcal{N}(T(x)) = \Phi_\mathcal{M}(x)\, C$. For an orthogonal $C$ (Theorem 5.3), multiplying by $C^\top$ gives $\Phi_\mathcal{N}(T(x))\, C^\top = \Phi_\mathcal{M}(x)$. Hence the recovery rule
$$
T(x) = \arg\min_{y} \big\| \Phi_\mathcal{N}(y)\, C^\top - \Phi_\mathcal{M}(x) \big\| ,
$$
a nearest-neighbour search among $n_\mathcal{N}$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$, done with a kd-tree.
:::

::: def
[Algorithm 5.7 — Spectral upsampling (ZoomOut)]{.tag} Melzi et al. (2019) start from a small $C$ of size $k_0$ and alternate:

1.  recover $T$ from $C$ (Proposition 5.6);
2.  recompute $C$ from $T$ with one more eigenfunction (Definition 5.2).

The map is refined while the basis grows; no descriptor is used after the first step.
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.8 — Matching two discretisations of a bumpy sphere]{.tag} Shape $\mathcal{N}$ is the same surface as $\mathcal{M}$, sampled with 1500 rotated Fibonacci directions instead of 1200. The ground truth is known through the directions. Errors are mean distances in units of $\sqrt{\text{area}}$.

```python
import numpy as np, scipy.sparse as sp
from scipy.sparse.linalg import eigsh
from scipy.spatial import ConvexHull, cKDTree

def bumpy(n, R):
    """Fibonacci directions rotated by R, triangulated, then pushed to radius r(d)."""
    i = np.arange(n) + 0.5
    phi, th = np.arccos(1 - 2 * i / n), np.pi * (1 + 5 ** 0.5) * i
    D = np.c_[np.cos(th) * np.sin(phi), np.sin(th) * np.sin(phi), np.cos(phi)] @ R.T
    F = ConvexHull(D).simplices
    r = 1 + 0.25 * np.sin(3 * D[:, 0] + 1) * np.cos(2 * D[:, 1] + 0.5) + 0.2 * D[:, 2] ** 3
    return D * r[:, None], F, D

def eig(V, F, k):
    n = len(V); I, J, W = [], [], []
    for a in range(3):
        i, j, o = F[:, a], F[:, (a + 1) % 3], F[:, (a + 2) % 3]
        u, v = V[i] - V[o], V[j] - V[o]
        c = (u * v).sum(1) / np.linalg.norm(np.cross(u, v), axis=1) / 2
        I += [i, j]; J += [j, i]; W += [c, c]
    W = sp.csr_matrix((np.concatenate(W), (np.concatenate(I), np.concatenate(J))), shape=(n, n))
    L = sp.diags(np.asarray(W.sum(1)).ravel()) - W
    area = 0.5 * np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V[F[:, 1]] - V[F[:, 0]], V[F[:, 2]] - V[F[:, 0]]), axis=1)
    m = np.bincount(F.ravel(), np.repeat(area / 3, 3), n)
    lam, phi = eigsh(L.tocsc(), k=k, M=sp.diags(m).tocsc(), sigma=-1e-6, which="LM")
    return lam, phi, m

def wks(lam, phi, q=40):
    """Wave kernel signature (Definition 3.10) at q log-spaced energies."""
    loglam = np.log(np.maximum(lam[1:], 1e-8))
    e = np.linspace(loglam.min(), loglam.max(), q); s = 7 * (e[1] - e[0])
    w = np.exp(-(e[None, :] - loglam[:, None]) ** 2 / (2 * s ** 2))
    return (phi[:, 1:] ** 2) @ w / w.sum(0)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Rb, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(3, 3)))
VA, FA, DA = bumpy(1200, np.eye(3))                # shape M
VB, FB, DB = bumpy(1500, Rb)                       # shape N: same surface, another sampling
lA, PA, mA = eig(VA, FA, 40); lB, PB, mB = eig(VB, FB, 40)
k = 20
gA = (PA[:, :k].T * mA) @ wks(lA, PA); gB = (PB[:, :k].T * mB) @ wks(lB, PB)
alpha = 1e-2 * np.linalg.norm(gA) ** 2 / np.linalg.norm(lA[:k]) ** 2
C = np.zeros((k, k))
for i in range(k):                                 # row-wise closed form (Proposition 5.5)
    C[i] = np.linalg.solve(gB @ gB.T + alpha * np.diag((lA[i] - lB[:k]) ** 2), gB @ gA[i])

truth = cKDTree(DB).query(DA)[1]                   # ground truth through the directions
def error(T):                                      # mean distance, in units of sqrt(area)
    return np.linalg.norm(VB[T] - VB[truth], axis=1).mean() / np.sqrt(mB.sum())

T = cKDTree(PB[:, :k] @ C.T).query(PA[:, :k])[1]  # Phi_N(T(x)) C^T ~ Phi_M(x)
print(f"random map: {error(rng.integers(0, len(VB), len(VA))):.3f}")
print(f"functional map, k = {k}: {error(T):.4f}, exact hits {np.mean(T == truth):.0%}")
print("diagonal of C (first 8):", np.round(np.diag(C)[:8], 2))
```

A random map has error 0.360. The functional map has error 0.0053, and 79 % of the vertices land exactly on the true vertex. The diagonal entries of $C$ have moduli $1, 1.23, 0.97, 0.89, 1.08, \dots$, close to 1 as Theorem 5.3 predicts. Their signs are arbitrary, because each eigenvector returned by `eigsh` is defined only up to sign; the descriptors fix them.
:::

::: note
[Note 5.9 — Symmetries, evaluation and basic matching]{.tag}

-   **Symmetries.** An intrinsic symmetry, such as the left–right flip of a body, is also an isometry; isometry-invariant descriptors cannot tell it from the identity. Making the bumpy sphere symmetric raises the error of Example 5.8 by a factor of about 25 (Exercise 10).
-   **Evaluation.** Benchmarks such as FAUST (Bogo et al., 2014) report the geodesic distance between predicted and true points, normalised by $\sqrt{\text{area}}$, as a mean or as a cumulative curve.
-   **Basic matching.** Matching each point to its nearest neighbour in descriptor space is the simplest method; it is noisy because descriptors repeat. Functional maps add the global, linear structure of Theorem 5.3, and the spectrum (Proposition 3.3) compares whole shapes.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   A pointwise map acts linearly on functions by pullback; in reduced bases it becomes a $k \times k$ matrix $C$ (Definition 5.2).
-   Isometries give an orthogonal $C$ that commutes with the eigenvalues: nearly diagonal, with signs to fix.
-   Descriptor preservation plus commutativity is a least-squares problem solved row by row.
-   Points are recovered by nearest neighbours between $\Phi_\mathcal{N} C^\top$ and $\Phi_\mathcal{M}$; ZoomOut refines while upsampling.
-   Intrinsic symmetries are the main ambiguity of intrinsic matching.
:::

## 6. Deep learning on curved surfaces {#ch6}

A convolutional network slides one filter over a grid, using translations and a fixed “up”. A curved surface has neither. This chapter builds surface convolutions from the spectrum, from local charts and from parallel transport.

::: note
[Note 6.1 — Three obstacles, and intrinsic versus extrinsic]{.tag}

-   **No translations**: the filter cannot be moved from point to point by a group action.
-   **No canonical orientation**: each tangent plane has a circle of possible reference directions.
-   **Varying discretisation**: the same surface comes with different meshes.

An **extrinsic** input (coordinates, normals) depends on the pose; an **intrinsic** one (built from the metric, like the HKS) is invariant to isometric deformations but blind to the embedding.
:::

::: def
[Definition 6.2 — Spectral convolution (Bruna et al., 2014)]{.tag} A **spectral convolutional layer** maps an input channel $x$ to an output channel through learned spectral coefficients $w \in \mathbb{R}^k$:
$$
y = \Phi_k\, \mathrm{diag}(w)\, \Phi_k^\top M x .
$$

It generalises Definition 2.8 by learning one coefficient per eigenfunction instead of a function of the eigenvalue.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.3 — What spectral filters depend on]{.tag}

-   If an eigenvalue is repeated and $w$ is not constant on its eigenspace, the layer depends on the arbitrary orthonormal basis chosen inside that eigenspace.
-   If $w_k = g(\lambda_k)$ for a function $g$, the layer is $g(-\Delta)$: it does not depend on the basis and commutes with isometries.

::: proof
A change of basis inside an eigenspace is $\Phi' = \Phi Q$, with $Q$ orthogonal and block diagonal on the eigenspaces. The layer becomes $\Phi Q\, \mathrm{diag}(w)\, Q^\top \Phi^\top M$. It is unchanged for every such $Q$ exactly when $\mathrm{diag}(w)$ commutes with every orthogonal block, that is when $w$ is constant on each eigenspace. The second claim is Proposition 2.9. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Across non-isometric shapes the $k$-th eigenfunctions are unrelated, so index-based coefficients do not transfer; coefficients that depend on $\lambda$ do. This is the idea behind the learned diffusion of [ch. 7](#ch7).
::::

::: def
[Definition 6.4 — Geodesic CNN and its variants]{.tag} The **exponential map** at $x$ sends a tangent vector $v$ to the end point of the geodesic of initial velocity $v$ and length $\|v\|$. Its inverse gives **geodesic polar coordinates** $(\rho, \theta)$ around $x$, valid within the injectivity radius.

A **patch operator** samples a signal $f$ on soft bins of this chart:
$$
(D(x) f)(\rho, \theta) = \int_S w_{\rho\theta}(x, y)\, f(y)\, \mathrm{d}A(y).
$$

The angle origin is arbitrary. The **geodesic CNN** of Masci et al. (2015) correlates a filter $a$ with the patch for every rotation $\theta_0$ of a discrete set, and keeps the best response (**angular max pooling**):
$$
(f \star a)(x) = \max_{\theta_0} \sum_{\rho, \theta} a(\rho, \theta + \theta_0)\, (D(x) f)(\rho, \theta).
$$

**Anisotropic CNNs** (Boscaini et al., 2016) orient anisotropic heat kernels along principal curvature directions; **MoNet** (Monti et al., 2017) learns Gaussian patch weights.
:::

To compare directional features at neighbouring points, a network must move tangent vectors between tangent planes: parallel transport.

::: def
[Definition 6.5 — Vector fields, parallel transport, holonomy]{.tag} A **tangent vector field** assigns to each point $p$ a vector $X(p) \in T_p S$. Along a curve $\gamma$, the **covariant derivative** of $X$ is the tangential part of $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} X(\gamma(t))$.

The field is **parallel** along $\gamma$ when this derivative vanishes, which defines a rotation $P_\gamma : T_{\gamma(0)} S \to T_{\gamma(1)} S$.

Around a closed loop bounding a small disk $\Omega$, transport rotates every vector by the **holonomy** angle, equal to $\int_\Omega K \,\mathrm{d}A$ modulo $2\pi$. On a curved surface, transport depends on the path.
:::

::: def
[Definition 6.6 — Discrete parallel transport]{.tag} Give each triangle $f$ a reference direction in its plane, its **frame**, and write a tangent vector as a complex number $z = r e^{i\theta}$, with $\theta$ measured from the frame.

Across an edge $e$ shared by triangles $f$ and $g$, unfold $g$ into the plane of $f$ by rotating it about $e$. The angle between the vector and the edge is kept, so
$$
z_f = e^{i \rho_{g \to f}}\, z_g, \qquad \rho_{g \to f} = \alpha_f(e) - \alpha_g(e),
$$
where $\alpha_f(e)$ is the angle of the edge direction in the frame of $f$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.7 — Holonomy around a vertex is the angle defect]{.tag} Transporting a vector once around the fan of triangles of an interior vertex $v$ rotates it by
$$
K_v = 2\pi - \sum_{f \ni v} \theta^f_v \pmod{2\pi}.
$$

::: proof
Unfold the fan triangle after triangle into the plane of the first one. Each transport is exactly this planar unfolding, so the transported vector is the same planar vector throughout.

The unfolded fan covers an angle $\sum_f \theta_v^f$ around $v$, so the copy of the first triangle reached after one turn is rotated by this angle with respect to the original. Identifying the two copies, the vector read in the frame of the first triangle has turned by $2\pi - \sum_f \theta_v^f$, modulo $2\pi$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Code 6.11 checks it at every vertex of a mesh.
::::

::: def
[Definition 6.8 — Gauges and rotation orders]{.tag} The choice of frames is a **gauge**. Rotating the frame of triangle $f$ by $\varphi_f$ changes the coordinate of a feature of **rotation order** $m$ into
$$
z_f \mapsto e^{-i m \varphi_f}\, z_f ,
$$
and the transport angles into $\rho_{g \to f} - \varphi_f + \varphi_g$. Scalars have order 0, tangent vectors order 1, line fields such as principal directions order 2.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.9 — Transported message passing is gauge equivariant]{.tag} For complex weights $w_0, w$, the layer
$$
(\mathcal{L} z)_f = w_0\, z_f + \sum_{g \sim f} w\, e^{i m \rho_{g \to f}}\, z_g
$$
satisfies $\mathcal{L}(z') = e^{-im\varphi} \mathcal{L}(z)$ for every gauge change $\varphi$. Without the transport factor, it does not.

::: proof
After the gauge change, each neighbour term becomes
$$
w\, e^{i m (\rho_{g \to f} - \varphi_f + \varphi_g)}\, e^{-i m \varphi_g} z_g = e^{-i m \varphi_f}\, w\, e^{i m \rho_{g \to f}} z_g ,
$$
and the first term is $e^{-im\varphi_f} w_0 z_f$. Complex multiplications commute, so the factor $e^{-im\varphi_f}$ comes out. Without transport, the factor $e^{-im\varphi_g}$ of each neighbour remains. [∎]{.qed}
:::

A non-linearity that acts on the modulus only, such as $z \mapsto \mathrm{ReLU}(|z| + b)\, z / |z|$, keeps the equivariance.
::::

::: note
[Note 6.10 — Invariant versus equivariant features]{.tag}

-   **Invariant** features (scalars, moduli $|z|$, angular max pooling) ignore the gauge but forget relative directions, such as whether a ridge runs along or across a bump.
-   **Equivariant** features rotate predictably with the gauge and keep this information until a last layer takes moduli.
-   **Harmonic surface networks** (Wiersma et al., 2020), the TP topic, apply filters $R(r)\, e^{i(m\theta + \beta)}$ in local polar coordinates to parallel-transported features, one stream per rotation order. Field convolutions (Mitchel et al., 2021) and gauge-equivariant mesh CNNs (de Haan et al., 2021) are related.
:::

::: ex
[Example 6.11 — Holonomy and gauge equivariance, numerically]{.tag} The code checks Theorem 6.7 at every vertex of a bumpy sphere, and Proposition 6.9 with $m = 1$ under a random gauge change.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial import ConvexHull

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 400
i = np.arange(n) + 0.5
phi, th = np.arccos(1 - 2 * i / n), np.pi * (1 + 5 ** 0.5) * i
D = np.c_[np.cos(th) * np.sin(phi), np.sin(th) * np.sin(phi), np.cos(phi)]
F = ConvexHull(D).simplices
flip = (np.cross(D[F[:, 1]] - D[F[:, 0]], D[F[:, 2]] - D[F[:, 0]]) * D[F].sum(1)).sum(1) < 0
F[flip] = F[flip][:, ::-1]                                     # outward orientation
V = D * (1 + 0.2 * np.sin(3 * D[:, :1]) * D[:, 1:2])          # a bumpy sphere

N = np.cross(V[F[:, 1]] - V[F[:, 0]], V[F[:, 2]] - V[F[:, 0]])
N /= np.linalg.norm(N, axis=1, keepdims=True)
X = V[F[:, 1]] - V[F[:, 0]]; X /= np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1, keepdims=True)
Y = np.cross(N, X)                                             # face frames (X, Y): the gauge

owner = {(t[k], t[(k + 1) % 3]): f for f, t in enumerate(F) for k in range(3)}
rho = {}                                                        # transport angle from face g to face f
for (a, b), f in owner.items():
    g, d = owner[(b, a)], V[b] - V[a]
    rho[(g, f)] = np.arctan2(d @ Y[f], d @ X[f]) - np.arctan2(d @ Y[g], d @ X[g])

angle_sum = np.zeros(len(V))
for k in range(3):
    p, q = V[F[:, (k + 1) % 3]] - V[F[:, k]], V[F[:, (k + 2) % 3]] - V[F[:, k]]
    np.add.at(angle_sum, F[:, k], np.arctan2(np.linalg.norm(np.cross(p, q), axis=1), (p * q).sum(1)))

first_face = {v: f for f, t in enumerate(F) for v in t}
gap = 0.0
for v, f0 in first_face.items():                                # walk once around each vertex
    f, hol = f0, 0.0
    while True:
        t = list(F[f]); g = owner[(v, t[(t.index(v) + 2) % 3])]
        hol += rho[(f, g)]; f = g
        if f == f0:
            break
    d = hol - (2 * np.pi - angle_sum[v])
    gap = max(gap, abs((d + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi))
print(f"max |holonomy - angle defect| over {len(V)} vertices: {gap:.1e}")

z = rng.normal(size=len(F)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=len(F))    # one tangent vector per face
def layer(z, rho, transport=True):
    out = 0.5 * z.copy()
    for (g, f), r in rho.items():
        out[f] += 0.3 * (np.exp(1j * r) if transport else 1.0) * z[g]
    return out
gauge = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, len(F))                      # rotate every face frame
z2 = np.exp(-1j * gauge) * z
rho2 = {(g, f): r - gauge[f] + gauge[g] for (g, f), r in rho.items()}
for transport in [True, False]:
    err = np.abs(layer(z2, rho2, transport) - np.exp(-1j * gauge) * layer(z, rho, transport)).max()
    print(f"transport = {transport}: equivariance gap {err:.1e}")
```

The holonomy matches the angle defect to $4 \times 10^{-15}$ at all 400 vertices. The equivariance gap is $10^{-15}$ with transport and 2.9 without.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   Surfaces lack translations, orientations and a fixed discretisation.
-   Spectral filters indexed by eigenfunction do not transfer; functions of the eigenvalue do.
-   Geodesic CNNs filter in polar charts, with angular max pooling or curvature for orientation.
-   Discrete transport keeps the angle to the shared edge; its holonomy around a vertex is the angle defect.
-   Transporting features before combining them gives gauge-equivariant layers that keep directions.
:::

## 7. Architectures and applications: from PointNet to DiffusionNet {#ch7}

Architectures for 3D shapes differ by the representation they consume and the invariances they build in. This chapter compares them and trains a small operator-based network.

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Global and local coordinate systems]{.tag}

-   **Global**: raw coordinates in a world frame. They are informative but depend on the pose; networks use random-rotation augmentation or a canonical frame from principal axes, whose signs are ambiguous.
-   **Local**: a frame per point (normal plus a tangent direction). Coordinates of neighbours in this frame are invariant to rigid motions, but the tangent direction must be chosen or made irrelevant ([ch. 6](#ch6)).
-   **Intrinsic**: quantities computed from the metric (HKS, WKS, geodesic distances), invariant to isometric deformations.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 7.2 — PointNet (Qi et al., 2017)]{.tag} A point set $X = \{x_1, \dots, x_N\}$ has no order, so PointNet computes
$$
f(X) = \gamma\Big( \max_{i} h(x_i) \Big),
$$
with $h$ and $\gamma$ multilayer perceptrons and the maximum taken coordinate-wise. $f$ is invariant to permutations, and every function of point sets in a compact domain that is continuous for the Hausdorff distance can be approximated uniformly by this form.

*Proof sketch.* Let $h$ return soft indicators of the cells of a fine voxel grid. The coordinate-wise maximum then records which cells are occupied, which determines the set up to the grid size. A continuous function of the set is approximated by a function $\gamma$ of this finite code. Zaheer et al. (2017) characterise the sum-decomposable version.
:::

PointNet sees each point alone before the maximum; local structure requires neighbourhoods.

::: def
[Definition 7.3 — Graph-based learning]{.tag} Build a graph on the shape, from the mesh edges or the $k$ nearest neighbours, and pass messages along it. EdgeConv (Wang et al., 2019) updates
$$
x'_i = \max_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} h_\theta\big(x_i,\ x_j - x_i\big),
$$
and recomputes the neighbours in feature space at each layer. Such networks depend on the connectivity: a remeshed shape is a different graph.
:::

::: def
[Definition 7.4 — MeshCNN (Hanocka et al., 2019)]{.tag} MeshCNN puts features on edges. The input is five numbers per edge: the dihedral angle, the two angles opposite to it, and two ratios of edge length to triangle height; they are invariant to rigid motions and scale.

Each edge has four neighbouring edges $(a, b, c, d)$ in its two triangles, known up to a symmetry. The convolution applies to the symmetric combinations $|a - c|$, $a + c$, $|b - d|$, $b + d$. Pooling collapses the edges of smallest feature norm, so the network simplifies the mesh where the task allows.
:::

::: def
[Definition 7.5 — SpiralNet++ (Gong et al., 2019)]{.tag} For meshes that share one connectivity, such as registered faces or bodies, each vertex gets a **spiral**: a fixed-length sequence of vertices starting at a chosen neighbour and turning outwards ring by ring. A layer concatenates the features along the spiral and applies a linear map, like a 1D convolution. It is fast and expressive, but tied to the template connectivity.
:::

::: def
[Definition 7.6 — DiffusionNet (Sharp et al., 2022)]{.tag} A DiffusionNet block takes per-vertex features $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times c}$ and applies three operations:

1.  **Learned diffusion**: each channel $c$ is diffused for a learned time $t_c \geq 0$,
    $$
    h_c = \Phi\, e^{-t_c \Lambda}\, \Phi^\top M\, x_c ,
    $$
